name: Bob Dylan
hook: A folk singer who wanted to be Little Richard, taught the Beatles that a pop song could be about anything, went electric in 1965, and later played his own song the way Jimi Hendrix had.
blurb: Bob Dylan was born Robert Zimmerman in Duluth, Minnesota, on 24 May 1941 and grew up in Hibbing. In his 1959 school yearbook he wrote that his ambition was to join Little Richard. He moved to New York in January 1961, was signed to Columbia by John Hammond that autumn, and became the best-known singer in the folk music scene, writing songs about war, racism and his own life that changed what a pop song's words could be about. George Harrison later described the Beatles wearing his records out, and John Lennon called 'You've Got to Hide Your Love Away' (February 1965) his own Dylan period. On 25 July 1965 he played with a loud electric band at the Newport Folk Festival. The story that the folk crowd booed him off is widely repeated, but accounts differ on how much booing there was, and on whether it was about the electric sound or the short set and bad sound mix. That summer his six-minute 'Like a Rolling Stone', produced by Tom Wilson, reached number two. Jimi Hendrix's 1968 recording of 'All Along the Watchtower' changed how Dylan himself played the song, and he has used Hendrix's arrangement since 1974. In 2016 he won the Nobel Prize in Literature. He has toured almost without stopping since the late 1980s and is still recording.
